title: Tenali and the Master of Animal Speech

keywords: tenali and the language of animals
full_text:
A pompous scholar named Pandit Shastrakavi arrived at King Krishnadevaraya's court, claiming he had attained supernatural enlightenment in the Nilgiri hills and had mastered the 'Universal Language of Birds and Beasts'.
'I understand every chirp of the sparrow, every bark of the hound, and every moo of the cow!' he boasted, demanding a monthly royal pension of two hundred gold dinars for his services as the Emperor’s Animal Ambassador.

King Krishnadevaraya, always fascinated by natural lore, was ready to grant the pension when Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, before we disburse royal gold, let us test the Pandit’s fluency before the court.'

Tenali sent a servant to the palace kitchens. The servant returned holding two animals: a hungry street dog and an aggressive alley cat, each secured in a separate wire basket.

Tenali placed the two baskets facing each other in the center of the hall, and pulled the wire latches.
The moment the cat saw the dog, its fur stood on end, its tail puffed up like a bottle-brush, and it let out a ferocious, spitting hiss:
*‘HIIISSS-FFFT-MREOOOWW!’*
The dog lunged forward, barking furiously:
*‘WOOF! WOOF! BOW-WOW-GRRR!’*

Tenali turned to the animal linguist:
'Learned Pandit! Translate their dialogue for His Majesty! What did the cat say to the dog, and what was the dog’s philosophical reply?'

The pretender began to stammer, sweating beneath his high turban:
'Ah... the cat said: "Peace be upon thee, noble canine brother, the weather is pleasant today!" And the dog replied: "Indeed, sister feline, may the gods grant thee good health!"'

Tenali burst into body-shaking laughter:
'Maharaj, hear the Pandit’s translation!
Any child in Vijayanagara knows that the cat said: "Keep away from me, you ugly hound, or I will claw your nose off!" And the dog replied: "Come down here, you spitting hairball, and I will chew your tail!"'

The King and the entire court erupted in uncontrollable laughter.
The pretender hung his head in humiliation, unable to utter another word.
King Krishnadevaraya dismissed the charlatan, warning him that in Vijayanagara, nature speaks for itself without the need of fraudulent translators.
moral: Pretenders who claim secret, unverifiable knowledge are quickly unmasked when tested with reality.
